items_missed: The move date was never asked. Not once in six minutes. The customer said 'I'm not sure if we're moving to that place but that's kind of what we're planning to move. So I'm giving it to next week to find out' — that is a one-week decision window and Calvin never asked when she needs the truck, never checked availability, and never gave her a reason to call back on a specific day. Everything downstream of this miss follows from it.

No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' The call goes from 'I got the email, and I'm looking at your kind of quote request' straight into 'so it's a two bedroom place or is three bedrooms.' No roadmap, no time expectation, no confirmation.

Neither address was collected — not the origin, not the destination. The customer named 'Converse' as the destination town and Calvin then told her 'There's no trip fees' without ever establishing whether Converse falls inside the San Antonio branch's free service zone. That is a pricing commitment made on an address he never asked for, and if a trip fee does apply it lands on a customer who is submitting this quote to a third-party payer as a fixed number.

Stairs were never probed. The customer stated both ends are two-story — 'a three bedroom duplex kinda like townhome. It's a three bedroom and then obviously, two story' going to 'a five bedroom, two story' — and Calvin never asked how many flights, where the heavy items sit relative to them, or whether the destination bedrooms are upstairs. Two two-story homes and zero stair questions, on a quote he then priced at the middle of a generic range.
The garage was volunteered and then dropped. She said 'some things in the garage' and got 'Mm-hmm.' Garage contents are the single most common source of unbudgeted hours and it was never scoped.

Box count was assumed rather than asked. Calvin told her 'we usually see about 45 boxes for a home the size' and built the estimate on that number without ever asking how many she actually expects. She later said she has been collecting free boxes from people, which suggests a real count was available for the asking.
Special considerations never probed — no long walks, no narrow hallways, no tight turns, on a duplex-to-house move with a three-piece sectional, bunk beds and a washer/dryer.
Access concerns never probed — no parking, no driveway, no HOA question at either end.
Storage stops and additional stops never asked.

The moving-stressor question was never asked, and the customer handed him the opening. She told an unprompted story about a previous mover who refused to move her piano on move day: 'that happened once with another place, they told me they were gonna move my piano. And then we got there, the guys were like, we don't move pianos. I'm like, your company said you did and so we had to leave it behind.' That is a customer telling you exactly what she is afraid of. The response was 'Mm-hmm. Sure, no problem.' The line that was sitting there — 'that's exactly what we make sure never happens, everything we commit to on the phone goes in your confirmation email so the crew shows up with the same information you have' — would have converted her worst prior experience into the reason to book Einstein.

The 'pricing is super simple' framing was there but the what's-included list was partial: 'There's no trip fees, there's no taxes. There's no credit card fees. We will pad and wrap all your items. Everything is fully insured and we also will have tools.' Gas and the truck itself were never named, and the no-hidden-fees pitch stopped short of the fuel surcharge and assembly fees.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.

The No Worries Damage Coverage explanation collapsed into confusion with her benefit cap. She said 'I think the state they cover a maximum of like $2,200 or 2500 for like moving expenses' and Calvin answered 'They cover $2,000 of the mo of up to $2,000 for a move,' then 'Oh, that's even more than what the estimate would be.' Two different $2,000s — her moving-expense benefit and Einstein's damage coverage — got tangled into one number, and she was left agreeing to something neither of them had actually separated. The coverage was eventually named correctly ('No worries damage coverage is included in the rate, it's higher valuation for your items') but never explained as repair, replace or reimburse, and never contrasted against the 60 cents per pound industry baseline.
No sense-check anywhere. The pricing, clock and estimate ran as one continuous block ending in a dollar range, and the customer's only interjection across it was 'Thank.'
Truck count was stated but drive time to Converse was never factored into the estimate, and no walk-distance question was asked at either end.

The Save Your Ass speech never happened, and this call handed him the setup twice. She said she is packing herself, and then: 'my main thing is like get whatever we can fit in the truck, hopefully everything. And then whatever we can, I can always just go back and grab those little things, you know, I have family I can help me.' She described the carload strategy herself and Calvin answered with 'Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.' The only prep content anywhere in the call was 'the loose miscellaneous items that don't get boxed add more time. So it's better to have more boxes than miscellaneous items' — a true statement dropped in the middle of a pricing block, not a prep speech, with no consolidation examples, no carload tip, and no 'does that make sense?'

No real booking attempt. 'So if you want to get on the calendar or anything we can also do that whenever you're ready' and 'you can just reach out when you're ready to get booked' put the entire next step on a customer who has not picked a house yet. He never offered to pencil in a tentative date, never set a follow-up call for after her decision, and never asked what day she would be calling back.

No bolded-details framing and no 'reply with any corrections.' Because this estimate is going to a third party who will pay the bill, the email is doing more work than usual and the verification ask matters more than usual — she said 'once you send me that I'll email it over to these people.' An estimate forwarded to a payer with an unconfirmed address, an assumed box count and an unasked move date is an estimate that will need to be reissued.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' and no hours or how-to-reach-us.
Customer's name used once — 'Hey, Lisa' in the greeting and never again.
top_strength: Calvin's pricing block is tight, correctly sequenced and lands the two differentiators most reps in this sample dropped entirely. In a single uninterrupted stretch he covered the simplicity opener, the crew and truck, the rate, the inclusions, the clock and the range: 'our pricing is really simple I'll be able to email this to you as well. But yeah, move this size. We send out one truck and two movers and our hourly rate is $192 per hour. Takes effect when they get on site. It's all inclusive. There's no trip fees, there's no taxes. There's no credit card fees. We will pad and wrap all your items. Everything is fully insured and we also will have tools and we can handle disassemble and reassembly. The way that it works is we do a two and a half hour minimum. And then following the minimum we bill in fifteen minute increments until the move is completed. So, you do just pay for the time used but typically a home this size will take two movers between six and eight hours. So, the typical cost range that we see is between $1,152 and $1,536.' That is the full clock section and most of the pricing section delivered cleanly in under a minute, with the range arithmetic correct and the time-based logic explicit. He then did something only one other rep in this week's sample did at all: he named the On-Time Guarantee unprompted — 'we do have an on time guarantee. So, if we're ever late to a window of arrival we do give you a money back' — and paired it with the no-deposit differentiator in the same breath: 'We don't have any deposits required to book or anything like that too. So if you want to get on the calendar or anything we can also do that whenever you're ready.' On-Time Guarantee has been hit on only 48 of 267 graded calls cumulatively, so this is a genuine bright spot. His opening handling of her actual ask was also sharp. She led with a procurement problem, not a moving problem — 'I'm having some company assist me. So, if you all gave me a quote, then you would give me like an invoice... I would have to have the invoice and stuff' — and Calvin answered it in four words before asking a single qualifying question: 'Yeah. We can do all that.' Removing the payment-mechanism worry first was the right read, and it is why she stayed on the phone.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is one line: ask for the date. This customer is choosing between two houses, expects to know 'next week,' and needs a written estimate to hand to a third-party payer — she is about as pre-qualified as an unbooked lead gets, and Calvin ended the call without a move date, without either address, and with the next step entirely in her hands: 'you can just reach out when you're ready to get booked.' The close that was available: 'Lisa, once you know which house it is, the date is what fills up fastest — what week are you targeting? I'll put a soft hold on it now, there's no deposit and no cancellation fee, so if the other house wins you just tell me and I move it or drop it. Costs you nothing and it means the date is still there when your answer comes.' That converts a no-deposit differentiator he already said out loud into an actual hold, and it gives him a reason to call her rather than waiting. Second priority: he has no addresses. He told her 'There's no trip fees' about a move to Converse without ever confirming Converse is in zone — and that quote is going straight to a payer as a fixed number. Get both addresses before the pricing block, every call, and especially when a third party is receiving the estimate. Third, the Save Your Ass speech is a near-total zero on a call that begged for it. She is self-packing, she said in plain words 'I can always just go back and grab those little things, you know, I have family I can help me,' and she is working against a hard benefit cap around $2,200. That is a customer who will do the prep work if you ask her to. 'Since you've got family helping and you're packing yourself anyway — everything small and loose that ends up in an armload instead of a box is what eats the clock. The stuff in drawers, the closet odds and ends, the pictures off the walls, the kids' toys. If you and your family take a carload or two over before we get there, that comes straight off your bill and keeps you under what the state will cover. Does that make sense?' That answers her budget constraint better than anything else on the call and it costs Einstein nothing. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-four review: this quote was built on an assumed 45 boxes he supplied himself, no addresses, no stair count on two two-story homes, an unscoped garage, and no drive time to Converse — then delivered as a hard range ($1,152 to $1,536) that is being forwarded to a payer. The known company pattern is underestimating the small end and padding the large end; this is neither, it is an estimate with no inputs, which is the version that produces the worst actuals-versus-booked variance because nobody can even diagnose why it missed. Worth pulling the actual against this one if it books. Finally, fix the insurance explanation — 'They cover $2,000 of the mo of up to $2,000 for a move' in the middle of a conversation about her state benefit cap left two different $2,000 figures fused together. The clean version separates them: 'That $2,200 is what your program will reimburse for the move itself. Separately from that, every Einstein move includes No Worries Damage Coverage — up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse accidental damage, at no extra cost. Most movers give you sixty cents a pound, which on a flat-screen is about twelve dollars.'
phone_presence_notes: Easy to talk to and never rushed — the opening 'Hey, Lisa, this is Cal at Einstein moving, how are you doing?' and the immediate 'Yeah. We can do all that' on her invoicing worry set a comfortable tone — but the warmth stayed at the level of acknowledgment rather than engagement: her name appears once in the whole call, her story about a previous mover refusing her piano drew only 'Sure, no problem,' and across three long customer monologues his side of the transcript is almost entirely strings of 'Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Uh-huh.'
